**Dry bulk freight — session/week and 1–8 quarter outlook (as_of 2026-09-09)**

**Current state (session/week)**

- BDI 3,620 on 9 September, +36 points day-on-day, up for a second session with support across all segments (OilPriceAPI reprint of Baltic Exchange assessments, data as of 2026-09-09; Hellenic Shipping News daily composite, 9 Sep). BCI 6,400 on 9 September (OilPriceAPI, 2026-09-09).
- The move is Capesize-led and demand-driven. BCI rose ~950 points week-on-week to 6,286 (7 Sep print), with average C5TC earnings up ~$8,600 to ~$53,500/day. C3 Tubarão–Qingdao hit a multi-year high of $41.55/mt on 4 September, roughly 70% above the September 2025 average of $24.50/mt (Hellenic weekly Capesize recap, published 9 Sep, data through 4–7 Sep).
- The rally is not a supply squeeze: ballaster counts rose in every segment week-on-week (Capesize +9% to 624, Panamax +10% to 820, Supramax +24% to 772), and the Capesize demand-to-supply pace indicator held at 1.05 — tonne-mile demand growing faster than available tonnage. That points to expanding demand rather than constrained availability (Hellenic weekly recap, 9 Sep).
- Segment split for the week to 4 September: BPI 2,448 (P5TC ~$22,035/day), BSI 1,675 (S10TC ~$19,143/day), BHSI 900 (HS7TC ~$16,199/day) (Hellenic weekly recap). Note BPI/BSI/BHSI are not in the OilPriceAPI catalog, so those prints are from the weekly recap only.
- BDI 3,628 on 4 September was described as a fresh high since October 2021 (Hellenic, 4 Sep). One caution: a Hellenic post dated 10 September (BDI 3,521, −99) is beyond today's as_of and is not used here.

**1–8 quarter outlook**

- BIMCO's July 2026 SMOO (published 29–30 July 2026, via World Cargo News reprint) is the current reference. It frames the outlook around two Strait of Hormuz scenarios: "SoH closed" (indefinite closure) and "SoH open" (reopening by end-Q3 2026). Under both, 2026 supply grows 1.5–2.5% — slower than fleet growth because of congestion and ~0.5% of the fleet trapped in the Persian Gulf — and demand outpaces supply: +2.5–3.5% under SoH closed, about one point higher under SoH open. BIMCO's line: the balance stays supportive in 2026 but weakens in 2027 from a high baseline, with demand growth slowing below supply growth in 2027 under both scenarios.
- El Niño is the new demand-side variable: expected to boost dry bulk demand over the next 12 months via Panama Canal transit restrictions (lengthening voyages) and a weaker Indian monsoon supporting coal imports (BIMCO, July 2026 SMOO).
- Geopolitical asymmetry: a full return of dry bulk to the Red Sea is not in either scenario and could cut tonne-mile demand ~2%; Houthi blockade announcements on Saudi Red Sea ports add uncertainty (BIMCO, July 2026).
- Supply-side watch: Capesize newbuilding orders reached 123 vessels in 2026 YTD, already above full-year totals of 103 (2024) and 115 (2025), ~117 at Chinese yards — supportive of owner confidence but additive to longer-term capacity (Hellenic weekly recap, 9 Sep). On Panamax, MSI's January 2026 view flagged 15–16m dwt of 2026 deliveries versus ~10m dwt in recent years, with a Q1 spike and a falling coal trade — a vintage from January, but the delivery schedule still applies to the 1–8 quarter window (Seatrade Maritime, 15 Jan 2026).
- Earlier in-year vintages for context: BIMCO's January 2026 SMOO had demand +2–3% and supply +2.5% for 2026 with Capesize outperforming; Geneva Dry's 2026 outlook (April) had 1Q26 ton-miles +5.2% YoY with Simandou ramp-up and firmer Australian/Brazilian iron ore flows. Both are superseded by the July SMOO for current-state work.

**Bottom line:** the current strength is real and demand-driven, concentrated in the Atlantic Capesize complex, with the composite at levels not seen since late 2021. The consensus 1–8 quarter view is constructive through 2026 — demand outpacing effective supply under either Hormuz scenario — with the balance expected to loosen in 2027 as supply growth accelerates and demand growth slows. The main swing factors are Hormuz/Red Sea access, El Niño effects on routing and coal demand, and the accelerating Capesize orderbook.

Sources: OilPriceAPI (BDI/BCI, data as of 2026-09-09); Hellenic Shipping News (daily composites 4–9 Sep; weekly Capesize/Panamax/Supramax recap published 9 Sep); BIMCO SMOO July 2026 via World Cargo News (1 Aug 2026); Seatrade Maritime (15 Jan 2026); Geneva Dry 2026 outlook PDF (April 2026).

**US Gulf grains on 63k Supramax — next couple of weeks (as_of 2026-09-09)**

**Where the tape is (Week 36, data through ~7 Sep)**

- BSI 1,675, +28 week-on-week; S10TC average $19,143/day, +$358 WoW. The strength is explicitly US Gulf-led: S1C (US Gulf–China/Japan) +$2,025 WoW and S4A (US Gulf–Skaw-Passero) +$1,512 WoW, while the Continent backhaul S4B eased −$397 (Hellenic Shipping News weekly Supramax recap, published 9 Sep, Baltic data as of 7 Sep).
- Prior week (Week 35, TSG Signal Group, published 3 Sep) put S1C at ~$30,356/day and S10TC at $18,785/day. So S1C is trading in the low-to-mid $30k/day band on a trip basis — very strong for the route, roughly $10k+ above the S10TC average.

**The key caution for the next couple of weeks**

- The rate spike is running ahead of the physical forward balance. Both Hellenic (Week 36) and TSG (Weeks 32–35) flag S4A/S1C as carrying a clear cumulative supply surplus across the forward window — i.e., more expected supply than expected demand on the very routes that spiked. The Supramax demand-to-supply pace indicator eased to 0.85 (Week 36, Hellenic) from 0.88 (Week 35, TSG) — demand growth lagging supply growth on a year-ago basis.
- Tonnage is building, not tightening: global Supramax ballaster count rose 24% WoW to 772, the largest build of any segment, led by the North Atlantic +44% (Hellenic, 9 Sep). TSG's net-vessel-supply work had the US Gulf/USEC as the highest-supply region for S4A/S1C. That looks like owners ballasting in ahead of the harvest season — which supports the market if cargo arrives to absorb it, and pressures prompt fixtures if it doesn't.
- Net read: the September S1C strength is partly pre-harvest positioning. That pattern has historically been absorbed once the corn/soybean export push hits, but it leaves prompt rates exposed to a give-back if loadings don't accelerate in the next 10–14 days.

**Physical cargo side (USDA)**

- The Gulf ocean cargo line-up is still running *below* last year: for the week ending 27 Aug, 18 grain vessels loaded in the Gulf (−47% YoY), with 29 expected in the following 10 days (−36% YoY) (USDA Grain Transportation Report, 09-03-26). US Gulf–Japan ocean freight $74.50/mt, +2% WoW — that series is the Panamax basis, but the direction corroborates the Gulf firmness.
- The supply side is beginning to ramp: barged grain movements were +41% YoY for the week ending 29 Aug (USDA GTR, 09-03-26). US corn/soybean harvest gets underway mid-September and the export push typically builds through October — that is the constructive case for your window into Q4.

**Tailwinds beyond the harvest**

- BIMCO's July 2026 SMOO (via World Cargo News, 1 Aug) flags El Niño over the next 12 months as a direct US Gulf–Asia grain angle: growing Panama Canal transit restrictions would lengthen US Gulf–China/Japan voyages (S1C ton-miles), and a weaker Indian monsoon supports coal import demand — both Supramax-positive. This is a 1–4 quarter factor, not a two-week one, but it is the reason the market is assigning a premium to Gulf ballast now.
- Keep the contradiction rather than averaging it: the demand/tone-mile narrative (BIMCO, TSG) is constructive, while the hard physical line-up (USDA) is below year-ago and the forward supply/demand balance on your routes is long. The two-week risk is primarily to the prompt S1C premium if the harvest ramp is slow to load; the October seasonal path is the bull case.

**Bottom line for the next couple of weeks:** you are in a seasonally favourable window — US Gulf firm, harvest starting, owners ballasting in for the autumn push — but the current rate level is not yet backed by the cargo line-up (Gulf loadings still ~36–47% below year-ago) and your specific routes sit in supply surplus on the forward curve. Expect high volatility around the S1C/S4A level with a bias toward a prompt give-back if loadings stay soft for another week; the October harvest acceleration is the event that decides whether the $30k+ S1C holds or extends.

Sources: Hellenic Shipping News weekly recap (Baltic data, published 9 Sep 2026); TSG Signal Group Weekly Dry Market Monitor Wk 35 (3 Sep 2026) and Wk 30 (29 Jul 2026); USDA Grain Transportation Report 09-03-26; BIMCO SMOO July 2026 via World Cargo News (1 Aug 2026).
